source_quality_note: Coverage combines Britannica overviews, ancient-source translations via LacusCurtius and Livius, UNESCO site material, and focused modern military/logistical analysis. Core dates and treaty terms are strong; speeches, casualty figures, motives, and anecdotes depend on later Greek/Roman literary sources.

verified_facts.fact: The Second Punic War followed Roman-Carthaginian rivalry after Carthage lost Sicily, Sardinia-Corsica, sea power, and indemnities after the First Punic War.
Hannibal’s strategy was to invade Italy, defeat Roman armies, and break Rome’s Italian alliance system rather than immediately besiege Rome.
After Cannae, Hannibal did not take Rome because he lacked siege machines and urban-assault enablers, faced Rome’s heavy defenses and walls, and had an exhausted, supply-limited army.
Scipio Africanus the Elder rose during the Second Punic War: extraordinary Spanish command in 210 BCE, capture of New Carthage in 209 BCE, victory at Ilipa in 206 BCE, and victory at Zama in 202 BCE.
Scipio Aemilianus, destroyer of Carthage in 146 BCE, was a later Roman commander distinct from Scipio Africanus the Elder.
The Battle of Zama was fought in North Africa, in modern Tunisia; Hannibal was defeated but survived and advised Carthage to seek peace.

The 201 BCE peace terms stripped Carthage of overseas possessions, limited its war fleet to ten triremes, required surrender of elephants, imposed a 10,000-talent indemnity over fifty years, and barred war without Rome’s consent.
Carthage recovered economically during the fifty-year gap after 201 BCE, even while its military and foreign policy remained restricted.
Cato the Elder repeatedly pushed the slogan remembered as 'Carthage must be destroyed' and helped normalize Roman hard-line policy.
The Third Punic War began after Carthage fought Masinissa’s Numidians without Roman permission, giving Rome a treaty-violation pretext.
In 149 BCE, Rome demanded Carthage surrender hostages and arms, then demanded relocation inland away from the sea; Carthage chose resistance.
In 146 BCE, Scipio Aemilianus captured and destroyed Carthage; survivors were enslaved and Carthaginian territory became Rome’s province of Africa.
Roman Carthage was later rebuilt on the ruins, and the archaeological site is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

debated_or_uncertain_facts.fact: Hannibal’s childhood oath of hatred toward Rome is a famous tradition, but it comes through hostile or later literary sources.
The exact battlefield location of Zama is debated, though North Africa/modern Tunisia is secure.
The exact wording and routine use of 'Carthago delenda est' are not preserved in a contemporary source; the sentiment is secure, the formula is later standardized.
Roman motives for the Third Punic War included security fears, revenge memory, economic jealousy, land hunger, domestic politics, and Masinissa’s disputes; weighting these motives is debated.
Ancient casualty numbers at Cannae, Zama, and the final siege vary by source and should be treated as approximate.
Reports that Scipio Aemilianus wept over Carthage’s destruction are ancient literary traditions but hard to verify as literal event footage.

myths_or_must_not_imply.myth: Do not state that Rome salted Carthage’s earth as fact; no ancient source supports it, and it is best treated as a later myth.
Do not imply Hannibal died at Zama; he survived, returned to Carthage, later went into exile, and died years later in the east.
Do not place Zama in Italy; it was in North Africa, in modern Tunisia.
Do not merge Scipio Africanus the Elder with Scipio Aemilianus; they belong to different generations and different Punic Wars.
Do not imply Cannae ended the war; Rome refused to negotiate and shifted to attrition.
Do not imply Carthage in 149 BCE was a Hannibal-era military superpower; it was economically revived but treaty-bound and militarily restricted.
Do not present Archimedes’ burning-mirror weapon at Syracuse as historical fact; Britannica notes it almost certainly did not exist.

historical_timeline.event: First Punic War ends with Roman victory.
historical_timeline.cause: Rome and Carthage fought over Sicily and western Mediterranean sea power.
historical_timeline.effect: Carthage loses Sicily and pays indemnity, creating pressure to rebuild power.

historical_timeline.event: Carthage fights the Mercenary War.
historical_timeline.cause: Unpaid mercenaries and African subjects revolt after the First Punic War.
historical_timeline.effect: Carthage survives but is weakened and politically humiliated.

historical_timeline.event: Rome takes Sardinia and Corsica from Carthage.
historical_timeline.cause: Rome exploits Carthage’s postwar weakness and mercenary unrest.
historical_timeline.effect: Carthaginian resentment deepens; Rome gains more western Mediterranean control.

historical_timeline.event: Hamilcar Barca begins rebuilding Carthaginian power in Iberia.
historical_timeline.cause: Carthage needs new wealth, manpower, and strategic depth after losing islands.
historical_timeline.effect: The Barcid power base in Spain becomes Hannibal’s launchpad.

historical_timeline.event: Tradition says young Hannibal swears hostility to Rome.
historical_timeline.cause: Hamilcar allegedly binds his son to the Barcid anti-Roman cause.
historical_timeline.effect: Later writers frame Hannibal’s career as inherited revenge.

historical_timeline.event: Hamilcar dies; Hasdrubal the Fair leads Barcid Spain.
historical_timeline.cause: Hamilcar is killed during campaigning in Iberia.
historical_timeline.effect: Hasdrubal consolidates rule through diplomacy and urban foundations.

historical_timeline.event: Ebro Treaty sets a Roman-Carthaginian boundary in Iberia.
historical_timeline.cause: Rome wants to limit Barcid expansion without immediate war.
historical_timeline.effect: Saguntum’s status south of the Ebro becomes a flashpoint.

historical_timeline.event: Hannibal becomes Carthaginian commander in Iberia.
historical_timeline.cause: Hasdrubal is assassinated and Barcid troops support Hannibal.
historical_timeline.effect: Carthage’s Spanish command turns aggressive under Hannibal.

historical_timeline.event: Hannibal besieges and captures Saguntum.
historical_timeline.cause: Saguntum is Roman-aligned and conflicts with Carthaginian interests south of the Ebro.
historical_timeline.effect: Rome demands redress; war becomes likely.

historical_timeline.event: Rome and Carthage enter the Second Punic War.
historical_timeline.cause: Carthage refuses Roman demands over Saguntum and Hannibal.
historical_timeline.effect: Rome prepares campaigns in Spain and Africa; Hannibal moves first.

historical_timeline.event: Hannibal crosses the Pyrenees, Rhône, and Alps into Italy.
historical_timeline.cause: He seeks to bypass Roman sea power and attack Rome’s alliance system in Italy.
historical_timeline.effect: His army suffers losses but shocks Rome by appearing in northern Italy.

historical_timeline.event: Hannibal wins at Ticinus.
historical_timeline.cause: Roman cavalry under Publius Cornelius Scipio probes Hannibal’s invading army.
historical_timeline.effect: Scipio is wounded; Gallic support for Hannibal increases.

historical_timeline.event: Hannibal defeats Rome at the Trebbia.
historical_timeline.cause: Consul Sempronius Longus accepts battle in harsh winter conditions.
historical_timeline.effect: Hannibal gains momentum and recruits more northern Italians.

historical_timeline.event: Hannibal advances through central Italy after a brutal march.
historical_timeline.cause: He aims to pull Roman armies into terrain of his choosing.
historical_timeline.effect: The maneuver sets up the ambush at Lake Trasimene.

historical_timeline.event: Hannibal destroys Flaminius’s army at Lake Trasimene.
historical_timeline.cause: Flaminius pursues without adequate scouting; fog and terrain hide Hannibal’s trap.
historical_timeline.effect: Rome panics and appoints Fabius Maximus dictator.

historical_timeline.event: Fabius Maximus adopts delaying strategy.
historical_timeline.cause: Rome needs time and must avoid another direct disaster against Hannibal.
historical_timeline.effect: Fabian attrition frustrates Hannibal but angers Romans seeking decisive battle.

historical_timeline.event: Battle of Cannae annihilates a massive Roman army.
historical_timeline.cause: Rome abandons Fabian caution and seeks decisive battle with superior numbers.
historical_timeline.effect: Rome suffers catastrophic losses; some allies reconsider loyalty.

historical_timeline.event: Hannibal does not besiege Rome after Cannae.
historical_timeline.cause: He lacks siege machines, urban-assault capacity, fresh supplies, and faces Rome’s walls and defenses.
historical_timeline.effect: He pivots to winning allied defections instead of storming the capital.

historical_timeline.event: Capua and several southern communities defect to Hannibal.
historical_timeline.cause: Cannae makes Hannibal appear unbeatable and promises a new power balance in Italy.
historical_timeline.effect: Hannibal gains prestige but not enough Latin allies to break Rome.

historical_timeline.event: Philip V of Macedon aligns with Hannibal.
historical_timeline.cause: Cannae encourages Rome’s enemies to test Roman weakness.
historical_timeline.effect: Rome fights a wider Mediterranean war while still containing Hannibal.

historical_timeline.event: Rome besieges Syracuse.
historical_timeline.cause: Syracuse shifts toward the Carthaginian side during Rome’s crisis.
historical_timeline.effect: Rome captures the city; Archimedes dies; Sicily returns firmly to Roman control.

historical_timeline.event: Rome besieges Capua; Hannibal marches near Rome as a diversion.
historical_timeline.cause: Rome targets Hannibal’s most prestigious Italian ally.
historical_timeline.effect: Romans refuse to abandon Capua; the city surrenders.

historical_timeline.event: The elder Scipio brothers die in Spain.
historical_timeline.cause: Carthaginian armies counter Roman pressure in Iberia.
historical_timeline.effect: Rome needs a new commander; young Scipio’s rise begins.

historical_timeline.event: Scipio Africanus the Elder receives extraordinary Spanish command.
historical_timeline.cause: Senior Roman commanders are reluctant after defeats; Scipio volunteers despite youth.
historical_timeline.effect: A new Roman strategic mind enters the war.

historical_timeline.event: Scipio captures New Carthage.
historical_timeline.cause: He attacks Carthage’s Iberian arsenal, treasury, hostages, and naval base.
historical_timeline.effect: Rome wins supplies, prestige, and Iberian diplomatic leverage.

historical_timeline.event: Scipio defeats Hasdrubal at Baecula, but Hasdrubal escapes.
historical_timeline.cause: Rome tries to destroy Barcid forces before they can aid Hannibal.
historical_timeline.effect: Hasdrubal marches toward Italy to reinforce Hannibal.

historical_timeline.event: Rome defeats and kills Hasdrubal at the Metaurus.
historical_timeline.cause: Hasdrubal crosses into Italy to join Hannibal for a direct threat to Rome.
historical_timeline.effect: Hannibal loses his best chance for major reinforcement.

historical_timeline.event: Scipio wins at Ilipa.
historical_timeline.cause: Rome seeks to finish Carthaginian power in Iberia.
historical_timeline.effect: Carthage loses Spain’s manpower, silver, and strategic base.

historical_timeline.event: Scipio becomes consul and argues for invading Africa.
historical_timeline.cause: Victories in Spain convince him Carthage can be forced to recall Hannibal.
historical_timeline.effect: Despite opposition, he prepares an African campaign from Sicily.

historical_timeline.event: Scipio invades North Africa.
historical_timeline.cause: He chooses an indirect strategy: threaten Carthage rather than chase Hannibal in Italy.
historical_timeline.effect: The war’s center shifts from Italy to Carthage’s homeland.

historical_timeline.event: Scipio defeats Carthaginian-Numidian forces near Utica and Great Plains.
historical_timeline.cause: Carthage and Syphax try to eject Scipio from Africa.
historical_timeline.effect: Syphax is captured; Masinissa’s position rises; Carthage recalls Hannibal.

historical_timeline.event: Hannibal leaves Italy and returns to Africa.
historical_timeline.cause: Scipio’s invasion puts Carthage itself in danger.
historical_timeline.effect: The two greatest commanders prepare for final confrontation.
historical_timeline.place: From Bruttium, Italy to Hadrumetum/Sousse, Tunisia

historical_timeline.event: Scipio defeats Hannibal at Zama.
historical_timeline.cause: Peace talks fail and Carthage risks one final field battle.
historical_timeline.effect: Hannibal survives but Carthage loses the war and seeks peace.

historical_timeline.event: Carthage accepts harsh Roman peace terms.
historical_timeline.cause: Zama leaves Carthage without a viable army.
historical_timeline.effect: Fleet is surrendered/destroyed except ten ships; indemnity and war restrictions bind Carthage.

historical_timeline.event: Scipio receives honors and the name Africanus.
historical_timeline.cause: His victory in Africa ends the Second Punic War.
historical_timeline.effect: Scipio becomes Rome’s model conqueror and a benchmark for later descendants.

historical_timeline.event: Hannibal becomes suffete and reforms Carthaginian finances.
historical_timeline.cause: Carthage must manage indemnity payments and internal corruption after defeat.
historical_timeline.effect: Carthaginian enemies and Roman suspicion push Hannibal into exile.

historical_timeline.event: Hannibal flees Carthage.
historical_timeline.cause: Political rivals accuse him of encouraging Antiochus III against Rome.
historical_timeline.effect: Carthage loses its greatest commander and avoids immediate Roman retaliation.

historical_timeline.event: Hannibal dies in Bithynia.
historical_timeline.cause: Rome pressures King Prusias to hand him over.
historical_timeline.effect: The living symbol of Carthaginian resistance disappears.

historical_timeline.event: Carthage economically recovers during the fifty-year gap.
historical_timeline.cause: Commercial networks, agriculture, and maritime trade continue despite military limits.
historical_timeline.effect: Rome grows jealous and fearful of a rich but treaty-bound Carthage.
historical_timeline.place: Carthage and North African hinterland, Tunisia

historical_timeline.event: Masinissa repeatedly pressures Carthaginian territory.
historical_timeline.cause: The 201 treaty favors Rome’s Numidian ally and restricts Carthage’s military response.
historical_timeline.effect: Carthage appeals to Rome but cannot stop Numidian encroachment.

historical_timeline.event: Cato visits Carthage and warns Rome about its revival.
historical_timeline.cause: Rome sends envoys amid Carthage-Numidia disputes.
historical_timeline.effect: Cato’s anti-Carthaginian campaign gains force.

historical_timeline.event: Cato repeats the demand remembered as 'Carthage must be destroyed.'
historical_timeline.cause: He sees Carthage as a revived danger close to Italy.
historical_timeline.effect: Hard-line Roman opinion overwhelms more moderate voices.

historical_timeline.event: Carthage completes its indemnity payments.
historical_timeline.cause: The fifty-year payment schedule from the 201 treaty expires.
historical_timeline.effect: Carthage is financially less constrained, heightening Roman anxiety.

historical_timeline.event: Carthage attacks Masinissa and loses near Oroscopa.
historical_timeline.cause: Numidian encroachment becomes intolerable and Carthage acts without Roman permission.
historical_timeline.effect: Rome treats the campaign as a breach of the 201 peace.

historical_timeline.event: Rome declares the Third Punic War.
historical_timeline.cause: Carthage’s unauthorized war against Numidia gives Rome a legal pretext.
historical_timeline.effect: Roman forces sail to Africa; Carthage first seeks surrender terms.
historical_timeline.place: Rome, Italy; Utica and Carthage, Tunisia

historical_timeline.event: Carthage gives hostages and surrenders weapons.
historical_timeline.cause: Carthage hopes obedience will prevent destruction.
historical_timeline.effect: Rome escalates demands after disarming the city.

historical_timeline.event: Rome orders Carthage moved inland away from the sea.
historical_timeline.cause: Rome wants to break Carthage’s maritime commercial identity permanently.
historical_timeline.effect: Carthage chooses total resistance and begins emergency rearmament.
